rationale: B wins because it keeps the set cleaner by protagonist: payer category, study evidence, money mechanics, and member service. A's best line, "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works," is sharper than anything in B, but A also trips over "demand for care exceeds clinician supply" after admitting no such fact was supplied. B's "Your health plan may now include Calm Premium at no cost. Here is how to check." adds a real consumer-service shape A missed, without pretending the facts are bigger than they are.
gaps_in_A: "at a moment when demand for care exceeds clinician supply" is an invented backdrop; the update gives no clinician-supply or unmet-demand data.
"on the plan's dime" overstates the payment mechanics when the update says no revenue terms were disclosed.
The category angle and insurer-protagonist angle are too close; both are payer-coverage stories unless one gets a named insurer executive with a real rationale.
It refuses "Mental health crisis meets a scalable solution" for lacking crisis and clinician-supply facts, then uses a softer version of that same unsupported context.
gaps_in_B: "pointing to a randomized trial as the reason" goes beyond the update; the facts say the study is being published, not that insurers relied on it.
The service angle needs insurer names and activation steps; without them, "Here is how to check" is a headline in search of usable service journalism.
"meditation apps cross from wellness perk to insurer-covered benefit" is a category claim built from one Calm deal; careful, or it becomes trend inflation.
The evidence angle is strong but labels itself "data" when the sharper editorial shape is the conflict-and-methodology story around company funding, self-reporting, and regular-user selection.
